modules.overview: The information boards need to oversee financial crime, how to read MI and dashboards critically, and how to obtain independent assurance rather than relying on assertion.
objectives: Specify the management information and indicators the board needs
Interpret financial crime MI and recognise false comfort
Obtain independent assurance from compliance monitoring and internal audit
syllabus: The core board information set: risk profile, alerts, backlogs and reporting
Key risk indicators: periodic review, screening, transaction monitoring and training
Recognising comfort without evidence and green dashboards
Compliance monitoring, internal audit and external reviews as assurance

modules.title: Culture, Conduct and Speaking Up
modules.overview: How tone from the top, incentives and the board's own behaviour shape whether staff report concerns and whether commercial pressure overrides financial crime controls.
objectives: Assess the firm's financial crime culture and the signals the board sends
Evaluate whether incentives and commercial pressure undermine controls
Identify how the board oversees whistleblowing and speaking up
syllabus: Tone from the top, the middle and the front line
Remuneration, sales incentives and accountability for breaches
Whistleblowing arrangements and the board's champion
Training and awareness that changes behaviour

modules.title: Supervisory Findings and Remediation
modules.overview: How the board responds when the authority identifies serious failings, oversees remediation and look-back exercises, and avoids repeat findings.
objectives: Explain how supervisors assess financial crime controls and escalate concerns
Evaluate remediation plans, independent reviews and look-backs
Challenge management on root causes, timelines and sustainable fixes
syllabus: Supervisory inspections, findings letters and risk mitigation programmes
Remediation governance: ownership, milestones and board reporting
Look-backs, independent reviewers and validation of closure
Repeat findings as a sign of a firm that is not learning

modules.title: Personal Liability and the Board's Action Plan
modules.overview: Brings the programme together into a board action plan, examining directors' personal exposure and how the board evidences effective financial crime oversight.
objectives: Assess directors' personal regulatory, civil and criminal exposure
Prepare the board to evidence its oversight to supervisors
Produce a board action plan for financial crime oversight
syllabus: Personal accountability, fitness and probity and enforcement against individuals
Reasonable steps: what the minutes and papers need to show
Board skills, training and external advice on financial crime
Workshop: the board's twelve-month financial crime oversight plan

programmes.title: Financial Crime Supervision in the Age of AI
programmes.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors to assess financial crime controls and firms' use of AI in monitoring, screening, fraud and surveillance.
programmes.intro: This training programme equips supervisory staff to assess firms' financial crime controls as AI transforms both detection and criminality: from AML/CFT foundations and sanctions to AI-driven monitoring, fraud and new generative AI typologies.
programmes.track: Pillar F: Reducing Financial Crime & Delivering Market Integrity

sections.Aim and Purpose:
To give supervisors a firm grounding in risk-based AML/CFT, sanctions and market abuse supervision, together with the technical understanding to assess firms' use of AI to detect financial crime. Participants leave able to challenge AI-driven monitoring and screening, recognise emerging AI-enabled typologies and form evidence-based supervisory judgements.

**Coverage:** The AML/CFT framework and risk-based approach, ML/TF typologies, supervising AML/CFT controls, AI in transaction monitoring, model risk in financial crime systems, sanctions and adverse media screening, fraud and behavioural analytics, generative AI typologies, market abuse surveillance, and bias, accountability and SupTech.
sections.Intended Audience:
- AML/CFT, sanctions and financial crime supervisors and inspectors
- Market surveillance, conduct and data analytics staff working on financial crime risk
- Senior managers shaping the authority's financial crime strategy and use of SupTech
sections.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the programme, participants will be able to:

- Explain the international AML/CFT framework and apply a risk-based supervisory approach
- Identify ML/TF, fraud and market abuse typologies and the red flags they leave
- Assess how firms use AI and machine learning in monitoring, screening and fraud detection
- Evaluate model risk, explainability, bias and human oversight in financial crime AI
- Challenge firms' resilience to new typologies enabled by generative AI
- Design the authority's supervisory response, including its own use of SupTech
sections.Syllabus:
### Module 1: The AML/CFT Framework and Risk-Based Supervision

The international foundations of AML/CFT supervision, the FATF Recommendations and mutual evaluations, and how authorities apply a risk-based approach to their populations of firms.

**Objectives**

- Explain the FATF standards and the supervisor's role within the national AML/CFT system
- Apply a risk-based approach to supervisory planning and resourcing
- Describe how mutual evaluations assess supervisory effectiveness

**Syllabus**

- FATF Recommendations, immediate outcomes and mutual evaluations
- National risk assessment, sector risk assessment and firm risk scoring
- Roles of the supervisor, the national FIU and law enforcement
- Regional AML frameworks and the move to supranational supervision

### Module 2: ML/TF Typologies and Red Flags

The main money laundering and terrorist financing typologies across banking, payments, investment and digital asset channels, and how to recognise red flags in real cases.

**Objectives**

- Identify key ML/TF typologies across sectors and channels
- Recognise red flags in customer, transaction and structural data
- Determine appropriate escalation when red flags are found

**Syllabus**

- Placement, layering and integration in modern financial channels
- Trade-based laundering, professional enablers and complex structures
- Terrorist and proliferation financing typologies
- Case study: tracing red flags through a laundering scheme

### Module 3: Supervising AML/CFT Controls in Practice

How to assess a firm's AML/CFT governance, business-wide risk assessment, due diligence and monitoring, and translate findings into consistent supervisory action.

**Objectives**

- Assess a firm's AML/CFT governance and business-wide risk assessment
- Evaluate customer due diligence, monitoring and suspicious activity reporting
- Apply consistent supervisory judgement and follow-up

**Syllabus**

- Board oversight, the AML compliance officer and management information
- Customer due diligence, enhanced due diligence and beneficial ownership
- Desk-based reviews, onsite inspections and sample testing
- From findings to remediation plans and enforcement referral

### Module 4: AI and Machine Learning in Transaction Monitoring

How firms move from rules-based to AI-driven monitoring using anomaly detection and network analytics, and the detection trade-offs supervisors should expect firms to manage.

**Objectives**

- Explain how AI and machine learning techniques are applied to transaction monitoring
- Assess claims about false-positive reduction and detection performance
- Challenge whether systems are tuned for detection rather than workload

**Syllabus**

- Rules-based versus AI-driven monitoring: capabilities and limits
- Anomaly detection, behavioural profiling and graph analytics
- False positives, false negatives and reading performance metrics critically
- Case study: an AI monitoring system under supervisory review

### Module 5: Supervising AI-Driven Financial Crime Systems

How to assess model risk management, validation, explainability and governance for AI systems deployed for AML/CFT purposes, including the human oversight that must accompany them.

**Objectives**

- Explain the model risk lifecycle for financial crime AI
- Assess validation, drift monitoring and explainability standards
- Evaluate ownership, sign-off and human oversight controls

**Syllabus**

- Model risk management expectations applied to financial crime AI
- Independent validation, back-testing and drift monitoring
- Explainability: balancing sophistication with the need to justify alerts
- Supervisory questions for a firm's AI model governance

### Module 6: Sanctions Screening and Adverse Media Monitoring

How firms meet sanctions obligations and use fuzzy matching and natural language processing for sanctions, PEP and adverse media screening, and how supervisors test calibration and control effectiveness.

**Objectives**

- Explain sanctions regimes and firms' screening obligations
- Assess the calibration and alert quality of AI-enabled screening tools
- Evaluate a firm's response to a potential sanctions breach

**Syllabus**

- UN, regional and national sanctions regimes and extraterritorial reach
- Fuzzy matching and NLP in name screening and PEP identification
- Calibration failures, list management and alert escalation
- Case study: a potential sanctions breach and the reporting response

### Module 7: Fraud Detection and Behavioural Analytics

How AI-enabled fraud detection works across payments and banking channels, from real-time scoring to behavioural biometrics, and how supervisors assess firms' fraud control frameworks.

**Objectives**

- Explain real-time fraud scoring and the data signals it relies on
- Identify payment fraud typologies, including authorised push payment fraud
- Assess the adequacy of a firm's fraud control framework

**Syllabus**

- Transaction, device and behavioural signals in fraud scoring
- Behavioural biometrics: strengths, limits and privacy considerations
- Authorised push payment fraud, account takeover and card fraud
- Criteria for assessing fraud controls and customer reimbursement

### Module 8: Generative AI and Emerging Financial Crime Typologies

How criminals use generative AI for synthetic identities, deepfake onboarding and large-scale social engineering, and the resilience firms and supervisors need to build.

**Objectives**

- Recognise financial crime typologies enabled by generative AI
- Assess firms' identity verification and liveness controls
- Challenge firms' resilience against AI-enabled social engineering

**Syllabus**

- Synthetic identity fraud and deepfake-enabled onboarding
- Voice cloning, deepfake video and AI-generated phishing
- Liveness detection, multi-factor verification and their limits
- Case study: a firm targeted by a deepfake-enabled fraud

### Module 9: Market Abuse Detection and Surveillance

How market abuse is detected through trade and communications surveillance, including AI-assisted tools, and how supervisors assess the adequacy of firms' own surveillance capability.

**Objectives**

- Explain the main categories and evolving typologies of market abuse
- Assess firms' trade surveillance systems and alert tuning
- Evaluate cross-market and cross-asset surveillance challenges

**Syllabus**

- Insider dealing, market manipulation and unlawful disclosure
- Spoofing, layering and cross-market manipulation
- Surveillance alerts, tuning and suspicious transaction reporting
- Case study: investigating a suspected market abuse alert

### Module 10: Bias, Accountability and the Authority's Own SupTech

Brings the programme together by examining fairness and accountability in financial crime AI and how the authority can use data and AI in its own supervision.

**Objectives**

- Assess bias and discriminatory outcomes in financial crime AI, including de-risking
- Evaluate audit trails and human-in-the-loop safeguards
- Design priorities for the authority's financial crime SupTech

**Syllabus**

- Bias sources, testing methods and remediation options
- Audit trails, accountability and customer impact of AI-driven decisions
- SupTech for AML/CFT: risk scoring, network analysis and data sharing
- Workshop: the authority's financial crime and AI action plan
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, grouped into three pathways and delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a technical briefing with case studies, red flags and supervisory question exercises, and pathways or individual modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of AML/CFT, sanctions or conduct supervision is helpful. No technical background in AI or data science is required.
sections.Core Reading:
- FATF, International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation: The FATF Recommendations (as updated)
- FATF, Guidance on Risk-Based Supervision (2021)
- FATF, Opportunities and Challenges of New Technologies for AML/CFT (2021)
- FATF, Guidance on Digital Identity (2020)

programmes.title: Financial Crises and Public Finances: Crisis Preparedness for Government
programmes.summary: An eight-module advanced programme preparing finance ministries and senior officials to manage financial crises, protect public finances and coordinate resolution.
programmes.intro: This training programme equips finance ministries and senior officials to prepare for and manage financial crises: understanding resolution regimes and safety nets, limiting the use of public funds, coordinating authorities and communicating under pressure.
programmes.track: G1. Financial Services Policy for Government

sections.Aim and Purpose:
To give the officials who will take decisions in a financial crisis a practical understanding of the crisis management toolkit, the finance ministry's role within it and the fiscal stakes involved. Participants leave able to assess national preparedness, take informed decisions on resolution and public support, coordinate with domestic and foreign authorities, and lead a credible crisis response under time pressure.

**Coverage:** How financial crises unfold and their fiscal costs, the finance ministry's role in crisis management, resolution regimes and the FSB Key Attributes, bail-in and loss allocation, deposit insurance and investor protection, public support, guarantees and state aid, liquidity support and funding in resolution, domestic and cross-border crisis management groups, simulations, and crisis communication.
sections.Intended Audience:
- Senior officials in finance ministries and treasuries with responsibility for financial stability and crisis management
- Members and secretariats of national financial stability and crisis management committees
- Legal, fiscal and communications advisers who would support ministers in a financial crisis
sections.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the programme, participants will be able to:

- Explain how financial crises develop and the channels through which they hit public finances
- Define the finance ministry's role and decision rights in a financial crisis
- Assess the national resolution regime, safety nets and funding arrangements against international standards
- Evaluate when and how public support should be provided and how losses should be allocated
- Design effective domestic and cross-border crisis coordination arrangements
- Lead crisis decision-making and communication through a realistic simulation
sections.Syllabus:
### Module 1: Anatomy of a Financial Crisis

How banking, market and sovereign crises develop, the warning signs that precede them, and the channels through which they damage public finances and the wider economy.

**Objectives**

- Explain the main types and triggers of financial crises
- Identify the bank-sovereign doom loop and other fiscal transmission channels
- Draw lessons from historical and recent crises

**Syllabus**

- Bank runs, contagion, fire sales and liquidity spirals
- Fiscal costs of crises and contingent liabilities
- The bank-sovereign nexus and market confidence
- Case studies of systemic and idiosyncratic failures

### Module 2: Crisis Management Architecture and the Finance Ministry

How responsibilities are divided between the finance ministry, central bank, resolution authority, supervisor and deposit insurer, and how decisions are taken when public funds may be at risk.

**Objectives**

- Map the roles and legal powers of each authority in a crisis
- Define the finance ministry's decision rights and veto points
- Assess the adequacy of national coordination committees and protocols

**Syllabus**

- Financial safety net participants and their mandates
- Decision rights where public funds or fiscal risk are involved
- Financial stability and crisis management committees
- Memoranda of understanding, protocols and escalation

### Module 3: Resolution Regimes and the Key Attributes

What an effective resolution regime contains, how resolution tools work, and how government can assess whether the national regime meets the FSB Key Attributes.

**Objectives**

- Explain the purpose of resolution and its objectives
- Describe the main resolution tools and powers
- Assess the national regime and resolution planning against the Key Attributes

**Syllabus**

- Resolution objectives and the public interest test
- Sale of business, bridge institutions, asset separation and bail-in
- Resolution planning, resolvability and loss-absorbing capacity
- Resolution of insurers, central counterparties and non-banks

### Module 4: Bail-In, Loss Allocation and Public Support

How losses are allocated to shareholders and creditors through bail-in, when public support may be justified, and how to design it to protect taxpayers and limit moral hazard.

**Objectives**

- Explain the creditor hierarchy and no-creditor-worse-off safeguard
- Evaluate the conditions for public support and the instruments available
- Design safeguards to recover public funds and limit moral hazard

**Syllabus**

- Bail-in mechanics, execution and market impact
- Recapitalisation, guarantees, asset purchases and nationalisation
- State aid principles, burden sharing and conditionality
- Recovering public funds and exit from public ownership

### Module 5: Deposit Insurance and Investor Protection

How deposit insurance and investor compensation schemes protect consumers and confidence, how they are funded, and how they interact with resolution.

**Objectives**

- Explain the design features of an effective deposit insurance system
- Assess coverage, funding and payout speed against IADI Core Principles
- Evaluate the role of investor and policyholder protection schemes

**Syllabus**

- Coverage levels, scope and depositor preference
- Ex ante and ex post funding and government backstops
- Payout readiness and the use of funds in resolution
- Investor compensation and policyholder protection schemes

### Module 6: Liquidity Support and Funding in Resolution

How central bank liquidity, government guarantees and resolution funds provide temporary funding in a crisis, and how to protect the public balance sheet when doing so.

**Objectives**

- Distinguish market-wide liquidity, emergency liquidity assistance and resolution funding
- Assess the role of fiscal backstops and indemnities
- Evaluate the risks to the central bank and public balance sheets

**Syllabus**

- Lender of last resort and emergency liquidity assistance
- Resolution funds and temporary public sector funding mechanisms
- Government guarantees of liabilities and their fiscal cost
- Collateral, indemnities and protecting the public balance sheet

### Module 7: Cross-Border Coordination and Crisis Communication

How authorities cooperate when a failing group spans borders, and how ministers and officials communicate with markets, depositors, parliament and the public during a crisis.

**Objectives**

- Explain the role of crisis management groups and cooperation agreements
- Anticipate cross-border conflicts over losses, assets and timing
- Design a crisis communication strategy and key messages

**Syllabus**

- Crisis management groups and institution-specific cooperation agreements
- Home and host tensions, ring-fencing and burden sharing
- Communication with markets, depositors, media and parliament
- Weekend resolution: timing, announcements and market opening

### Module 8: Crisis Simulation and Preparedness Planning

Brings the programme together in a realistic crisis simulation in which participants take decisions under time pressure, followed by a review of national preparedness and an action plan.

**Objectives**

- Apply the crisis toolkit to a realistic failing-institution scenario
- Identify gaps in powers, information, funding and coordination
- Produce a national crisis preparedness action plan

**Syllabus**

- Designing and running crisis simulation exercises
- Simulation: a failing systemic institution over a resolution weekend
- Debrief: decisions, information gaps and coordination lessons
- Workshop: a national crisis preparedness action plan
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as an intensive programme over two to three days or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a briefing with crisis case studies and decision exercises, culminating in a full crisis simulation, and modules can be selected or tailored to the national crisis management framework.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Experience of financial stability, fiscal or financial sector policy is helpful. No prior crisis management experience is required.
sections.Core Reading:
- FSB (2014), Key Attributes of Effective Resolution Regimes for Financial Institutions
- IADI (2014), IADI Core Principles for Effective Deposit Insurance Systems
- FSB (2016), Guiding Principles on the Temporary Funding Needed to Support the Orderly Resolution of a Global Systemically Important Bank
- FSB (2018), Principles on Bail-in Execution

programmes.title: Financial Inclusion and Consumer Protection Policy
programmes.summary: An eight-module programme helping policymakers widen access to financial services while protecting consumers through strategy, regulation, redress and fraud prevention.
programmes.intro: This training programme equips ministries, legislators and public agencies to design policy that widens access to financial services while protecting consumers: inclusion strategies, digital finance, financial literacy, consumer protection frameworks, redress and the fight against fraud and scams.
programmes.track: G1. Financial Services Policy for Government

sections.Aim and Purpose:
To give policymakers a practical understanding of how to expand access to useful, affordable financial services and how to protect consumers once they use them. Participants leave able to design a national financial inclusion strategy, strengthen the consumer protection framework, set up effective complaints and redress arrangements, and respond to the growing threat of fraud and scams.

**Coverage:** Measuring financial access and exclusion, national financial inclusion strategies, digital financial services and mobile money, digital identity and proportionate customer due diligence, financial literacy and capability strategies, consumer protection frameworks and institutional models, complaints handling and ombudsman schemes, fraud and scams, and evaluating policy impact.
sections.Intended Audience:
- Officials in finance ministries, treasuries and central banks responsible for financial inclusion and consumer policy
- Staff of consumer protection agencies, ombudsman schemes and financial education bodies
- Legislative drafters, legal advisers and parliamentary committee staff working on consumer and financial inclusion legislation
sections.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the programme, participants will be able to:

- Measure financial access, usage and exclusion and identify the groups most affected
- Design a national financial inclusion strategy with clear targets and governance
- Assess the opportunities and risks of digital financial services for inclusion
- Develop a national financial literacy and capability strategy
- Evaluate consumer protection frameworks, institutional models and redress arrangements
- Design a coordinated policy response to fraud and scams
sections.Syllabus:
### Module 1: Financial Inclusion: Evidence and Barriers

Why financial inclusion matters for growth and resilience, how access and usage are measured, and the economic, social and regulatory barriers that keep people excluded.

**Objectives**

- Explain the economic and social case for financial inclusion
- Use demand-side and supply-side data to measure access and usage
- Identify the barriers facing women, rural, low-income and other excluded groups

**Syllabus**

- Inclusion, growth, resilience and poverty reduction
- Global Findex and national survey data
- Barriers: cost, distance, documentation, trust and capability
- Gender gaps, small businesses and forcibly displaced people

### Module 2: National Financial Inclusion Strategies

How to develop, govern and implement a national financial inclusion strategy, setting priorities and targets and aligning ministries, regulators and the private sector.

**Objectives**

- Design the structure, priorities and targets of a national strategy
- Establish governance and coordination for implementation
- Monitor progress with a results framework

**Syllabus**

- Diagnostics, stakeholder engagement and priority setting
- Governance: steering committees, working groups and secretariats
- Public sector levers: government payments, postal networks and state banks
- Results frameworks, targets and reporting

### Module 3: Digital Finance, Mobile Money and Digital Public Infrastructure

How mobile money, agent networks, digital identity and fast payment systems have transformed access, and the regulatory choices that enable them while managing new risks.

**Objectives**

- Explain how digital financial services expand access
- Assess enabling regulation for e-money, agents and digital credit
- Evaluate the role of digital identity and proportionate customer due diligence

**Syllabus**

- Mobile money, agent networks and interoperability
- Digital credit, buy now pay later and over-indebtedness
- Digital identity, tiered due diligence and FATF guidance on inclusion
- Digital public infrastructure and government-to-person payments

### Module 4: Financial Literacy and Capability Strategies

How to design a national strategy to improve financial literacy and capability, what evidence shows about what works, and how to reach different audiences effectively.

**Objectives**

- Explain the OECD framework for national financial literacy strategies
- Assess the evidence on effective financial education interventions
- Design programmes for schools, adults, small businesses and vulnerable groups

**Syllabus**

- National strategy design, governance and stakeholder roles
- Measuring financial literacy and capability
- Behavioural insights and teachable moments
- Digital financial literacy and scam awareness

### Module 5: Consumer Protection Frameworks and Institutions

The legal and institutional foundations of financial consumer protection, the international principles that guide them, and the choices in assigning responsibilities to regulators.

**Objectives**

- Explain the G20/OECD High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection
- Compare institutional models for financial consumer protection
- Assess gaps in disclosure, fair treatment, product and conduct rules

**Syllabus**

- Disclosure, transparency of costs and fair treatment
- Responsible lending, product governance and suitability
- Institutional models: integrated, twin peaks and dedicated agencies
- Data protection, privacy and vulnerable consumers

### Module 6: Complaints, Redress and Ombudsman Schemes

How to give consumers effective routes to redress, from internal complaints handling to independent ombudsman schemes, and how complaints data can inform policy and supervision.

**Objectives**

- Set standards for internal complaints handling by firms
- Design an independent, accessible and fair ombudsman scheme
- Use complaints data to identify emerging harm

**Syllabus**

- Internal dispute resolution standards
- Ombudsman scheme design: independence, jurisdiction, funding and binding decisions
- Mass redress, collective actions and compensation schemes
- Complaints data as an early warning system

### Module 7: Fraud, Scams and Consumer Harm

The rapid growth of authorised push payment fraud, investment scams and online financial harm, and the policy tools to prevent fraud, allocate liability and support victims.

**Objectives**

- Describe the main fraud and scam typologies affecting consumers
- Evaluate prevention, reimbursement and liability allocation policies
- Design coordination between regulators, law enforcement, telecoms and online platforms

**Syllabus**

- Investment, romance, impersonation and authorised push payment scams
- Reimbursement and liability models for payment fraud
- Online platforms, telecoms and advertising controls
- National fraud strategies and victim support

### Module 8: Balancing Inclusion, Protection and Innovation

Brings the programme together by examining the trade-offs between inclusion, protection, stability and integrity, and building an integrated policy action plan.

**Objectives**

- Weigh trade-offs between inclusion, consumer protection and financial integrity
- Evaluate policy impact using evidence and data
- Produce an integrated inclusion and consumer protection action plan

**Syllabus**

- Proportionality and the inclusion, stability, integrity and protection balance
- Sandboxes and innovation in inclusive finance
- Impact evaluation and course correction
- Workshop: an inclusion and consumer protection action plan

programmes.title: Financial Investigation: Following the Money
programmes.summary: A ten-module programme equipping investigators and analysts to run parallel financial investigations, trace funds through accounts and corporate vehicles, and present financial evidence.
programmes.intro: This training programme equips investigators and analysts to run parallel financial investigations that identify criminal proceeds, trace money through accounts and corporate vehicles, and present financial evidence that stands up in court.

sections.Aim and Purpose:
To give investigators and analysts the methods to make financial investigation a routine part of every case involving profit-generating crime. Participants leave able to obtain and analyse financial records, unpick corporate structures, calculate criminal benefit and present clear, defensible findings to prosecutors and the court.

**Coverage:** The purpose and principles of financial investigation, planning parallel investigations, sources of financial information, production orders and other powers, analysing bank and payment records, cash and informal value transfer, net-worth and source-and-application-of-funds analysis, corporate vehicles and beneficial ownership, digital and crypto-asset evidence, and presenting financial findings.
sections.Intended Audience:
- Police and agency investigators handling acquisitive, organised or economic crime
- Financial investigators, intelligence analysts and FIU staff supporting investigations
- Asset recovery, customs and tax investigators who trace and evidence criminal finances
sections.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the programme, participants will be able to:

- Explain the purpose of parallel financial investigation and when to start one
- Identify and obtain financial information lawfully using the appropriate powers
- Analyse bank, payment and cash records to establish money flows and patterns
- Apply net-worth and source-and-application-of-funds methods to evidence criminal benefit
- Trace funds through companies, trusts and nominees to their beneficial owners
- Present financial findings clearly to prosecutors, courts and partner agencies
sections.Syllabus:
### Module 1: Financial Investigation: Purpose and Principles

Why every profit-generating crime should have a financial dimension, the objectives a financial investigation can serve, and what the FATF standards expect of investigative authorities.

**Objectives**

- Explain the evidential, intelligence and asset recovery purposes of financial investigation
- Distinguish parallel financial investigations from stand-alone money laundering cases
- Summarise the FATF expectations for investigative powers and outcomes

**Syllabus**

- Following the money: proving offences, finding assets and mapping networks
- Parallel financial investigation alongside predicate offence cases
- FATF Recommendations 30 and 31 and Immediate Outcome 7
- The financial investigator's role in a multi-disciplinary team

### Module 2: Planning and Managing a Financial Investigation

How to scope a financial investigation, set objectives and hypotheses, prioritise lines of enquiry and manage records, exhibits and disclosure from the outset.

**Objectives**

- Set investigation objectives, hypotheses and a lines-of-enquiry plan
- Prioritise enquiries in proportion to risk and resources
- Maintain decision logs, exhibits and audit trails from the start

**Syllabus**

- Scoping: subjects, periods, predicate offences and assets
- Investigation plans, hypotheses and lines of enquiry
- Coordination with intelligence, asset recovery and prosecutors
- Record-keeping, decision logs and early disclosure planning

### Module 3: Sources of Financial Information

The open, closed and restricted sources investigators can use to build a financial profile, and how to assess their reliability and the conditions attached to their use.

**Objectives**

- Identify open, closed and restricted sources of financial information
- Assess reliability, completeness and handling conditions
- Build an initial financial profile of a subject

**Syllabus**

- Public registers: companies, land, vehicles and court records
- FIU intelligence and tax, customs and law-enforcement holdings
- Open-source research and lifestyle indicators
- Building the subject's financial profile

### Module 4: Investigative Powers: Production Orders and Beyond

The legal tools for obtaining financial records and information, how to draft applications that are precise and justified, and how to work effectively with the institutions that must comply.

**Objectives**

- Explain the main powers to obtain financial information and their thresholds
- Draft focused, justified applications for production and disclosure orders
- Manage institution responses, deadlines and data formats

**Syllabus**

- Production, disclosure, account monitoring and customer information orders
- Search, seizure and powers to obtain electronic records
- Drafting applications: necessity, proportionality and specificity
- Working with institutions: contacts, formats and confidentiality

### Module 5: Analysing Bank and Payment Records

Techniques for reading and analysing account statements, payment data and supporting documents to identify patterns, links and anomalies that test the investigation's hypotheses.

**Objectives**

- Read account opening, statement and payment records accurately
- Apply spreadsheet and analytical techniques to large transaction sets
- Identify patterns indicating laundering, fraud or hidden assets

**Syllabus**

- Account opening files, statements, payment messages and card data
- Cleaning, normalising and reconciling transaction data
- Pattern analysis: round sums, pass-through activity and structuring
- Charting money flows and counterparties

### Module 6: Cash, Value Transfer and Alternative Remittance

How criminal cash is moved, stored and converted, how informal value transfer and alternative remittance operate, and the evidence investigators can obtain about them.

**Objectives**

- Explain how cash proceeds are placed and moved
- Describe informal value transfer and alternative remittance systems
- Identify evidence sources for cash-based and informal transfers

**Syllabus**

- Cash-intensive businesses and cash deposits
- Cross-border cash movements and declarations
- Informal value transfer and alternative remittance
- Evidencing cash: seizures, ledgers and communications

### Module 7: Net-Worth and Source-and-Application-of-Funds Analysis

Indirect methods for proving unexplained income and wealth, how to build a defensible net-worth or source-and-application-of-funds analysis, and how these support charges and confiscation.

**Objectives**

- Explain when indirect methods of proof are appropriate
- Build a net-worth and a source-and-application-of-funds statement
- Test the analysis against likely defence explanations

**Syllabus**

- Direct versus indirect methods of proof
- Net-worth method: assets, liabilities, expenditure and known income
- Source-and-application-of-funds statements
- Anticipating defences: cash savings, gifts, loans and inheritances

### Module 8: Corporate Vehicles and Beneficial Ownership

How companies, trusts, foundations and nominees are used to conceal ownership and move funds, and how investigators trace control through registers, records and cooperation.

**Objectives**

- Recognise how legal persons and arrangements are misused to conceal ownership
- Trace control and beneficial ownership using registers and institution records
- Identify the role of professional enablers

**Syllabus**

- Shell, shelf and front companies, trusts and nominee arrangements
- Beneficial ownership registers, service provider records and their limits
- Mapping ownership and control across jurisdictions
- Professional enablers: lawyers, accountants and company service providers

### Module 9: Digital Payments and Crypto-Asset Evidence

Obtaining and interpreting evidence from payment firms, e-money issuers, online platforms and crypto-asset service providers, and integrating it with traditional financial records.

**Objectives**

- Identify the records held by payment, e-money and crypto-asset service providers
- Integrate digital payment and blockchain data into the financial picture
- Recognise the evidential limits of analytics outputs

**Syllabus**

- Payment firms, e-money accounts and online marketplaces
- Crypto-asset service provider records and blockchain tracing basics
- Device, communications and other digital financial evidence
- Attribution, reliability and continuity of digital evidence

### Module 10: Presenting Financial Findings: Investigation Workshop

Brings the programme together in a case exercise in which teams analyse records, trace funds through corporate vehicles, calculate benefit and present their findings to a mock prosecution review.

**Objectives**

- Prepare clear financial statements, charts and summaries for prosecutors and courts
- Explain analysis and assumptions under challenge
- Apply the programme's methods to a realistic case

**Syllabus**

- Writing financial investigation reports and witness statements
- Charts, schedules and summaries that courts can follow
- Giving evidence and handling cross-examination on financial analysis
- Workshop: tracing, benefit calculation and case presentation
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a technical briefing with worked records and case exercises, ending in an investigation workshop, and modules can be selected or tailored to the participants' roles and caseload.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of criminal investigation, intelligence analysis or financial crime work is helpful. No accounting qualification is required.
sections.Core Reading:
- FATF (2012), Operational Issues: Financial Investigations Guidance
- FATF (2012, as updated), International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation: The FATF Recommendations
- FATF and Egmont Group (2018), Concealment of Beneficial Ownership
- FATF (2023), Guidance on Beneficial Ownership for Legal Persons
- FATF (2018), Professional Money Laundering

programmes.title: Financial Services Regulation: A Briefing Programme for Parliamentarians
programmes.summary: A six-module, non-technical briefing programme helping parliamentarians and committee staff scrutinise financial legislation and hold regulators to account.
programmes.intro: This training programme equips parliamentarians and committee staff with a clear, non-technical understanding of how financial regulation works, so they can scrutinise legislation, hold regulators to account and respond to emerging issues with confidence.
programmes.track: G1. Financial Services Policy for Government

sections.Aim and Purpose:
To give legislators and their staff a concise, jargon-free briefing on financial services regulation, the role of independent regulators and the issues that come before parliament. Participants leave able to ask incisive questions of regulators and ministers, scrutinise financial legislation effectively and judge emerging issues such as crypto-assets and AI.

**Coverage:** How financial regulation works and who does what, holding independent regulators to account, scrutinising financial legislation, consumer protection and lessons from financial scandals, financial crime and the country's international obligations, and emerging issues including crypto-assets and AI.
sections.Intended Audience:
- Members of parliament, particularly those on finance, economic affairs, budget and public accounts committees
- Committee clerks, researchers and parliamentary library staff supporting financial scrutiny
- Advisers to parliamentarians and party policy staff working on financial issues
sections.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the programme, participants will be able to:

- Explain in plain language why financial services are regulated and who does what
- Hold regulators to account while respecting their operational independence
- Scrutinise financial legislation and the powers it confers
- Draw lessons from financial scandals for consumer protection policy
- Explain the country's financial crime obligations and how they are assessed internationally
- Ask informed questions about emerging issues such as crypto-assets and AI
sections.Syllabus:
### Module 1: How Financial Regulation Works

Why financial services are regulated, the institutions responsible, and how international standards shape national rules, explained without jargon.

**Objectives**

- Explain the purposes of financial regulation
- Identify the roles of the ministry, central bank, regulators and other bodies
- Describe how international standards influence national law

**Syllabus**

- What can go wrong in finance and why it matters to constituents
- Who regulates what: the national regulatory map
- International standard-setters and peer reviews
- Key terms every legislator should know

### Module 2: Holding Regulators to Account

Why regulators are given independence, the accountability mechanisms parliament controls, and how to conduct effective scrutiny hearings and inquiries.

**Objectives**

- Explain the rationale for regulatory independence and its limits
- Use annual reports, hearings and inquiries to scrutinise regulators
- Distinguish legitimate scrutiny from interference in individual cases

**Syllabus**

- Independence, mandates and appointments
- Annual reports, budgets and performance information
- Preparing for and conducting a scrutiny hearing
- A question set for regulators and ministers

### Module 3: Scrutinising Financial Legislation

How financial bills are structured, what to look for in the powers and safeguards they contain, and how to test impact assessments and industry claims.

**Objectives**

- Identify the main components of a financial services bill
- Assess delegated powers, safeguards and review clauses
- Test impact assessments, consultation responses and lobbying claims

**Syllabus**

- Perimeter, licensing, enforcement and transitional provisions explained
- Delegated powers and parliamentary oversight of rules
- Reading an impact assessment critically
- Engaging with industry and consumer representations

### Module 4: Consumer Protection and Lessons from Scandals

How consumer protection in finance is meant to work, what recent mis-selling and fraud scandals reveal about regulatory failure, and the remedies available to consumers.

**Objectives**

- Describe the main consumer protection tools and redress mechanisms
- Draw lessons from mis-selling and fraud scandals
- Assess whether consumers can obtain effective redress

**Syllabus**

- Disclosure, suitability, fair treatment and product rules
- Case studies of mis-selling, investment fraud and firm failures
- Ombudsman schemes, compensation and deposit protection
- Constituency casework: helping consumers who have lost money

### Module 5: Financial Crime and International Obligations

The country's obligations to combat money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion, how they are assessed by the FATF, and what is at stake for the economy.

**Objectives**

- Explain the FATF standards and the mutual evaluation process
- Describe the consequences of grey-listing for the economy
- Identify the legislative role in beneficial ownership and asset recovery

**Syllabus**

- Money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions explained
- FATF evaluations, grey-listing and its economic impact
- Beneficial ownership transparency and asset recovery laws
- Scams and fraud as a growing financial crime threat

### Module 6: Emerging Issues: Crypto-Assets, AI and the Future of Finance

Brings the programme together by examining emerging issues likely to come before parliament, including crypto-assets, stablecoins, AI, climate risk and cyber threats.

**Objectives**

- Explain crypto-assets, stablecoins and AI in plain language
- Assess the main risks and regulatory options for emerging issues
- Prepare a scrutiny agenda for the parliamentary term

**Syllabus**

- Crypto-assets and stablecoins: risks and regulatory approaches
- AI in finance: benefits, risks and accountability
- Climate risk, cyber threats and operational resilience
- Workshop: a committee scrutiny agenda on financial services
sections.Structure and Format: Six modules of about two hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a two-day programme or as a series of short briefing sessions around the parliamentary timetable. Each module combines a plain-language briefing with a case study and a scrutiny question set, and modules can be selected or tailored to committee priorities.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: No prior knowledge of financial services or regulation is required. Experience of committee work is helpful.
sections.Core Reading:
- OECD (2014), The Governance of Regulators, OECD Best Practice Principles for Regulatory Policy
- G20/OECD (2022), High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection
- FATF (2012, updated), International Standards on Combating Money Laundering and the Financing of Terrorism and Proliferation: The FATF Recommendations
- IOSCO (2017), Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation

FATF evaluations, grey-listing and its economic impact

Scams and fraud as a growing financial crime threat

programmes.title: Financial Services Policy Essentials for Government
programmes.summary: A ten-module programme giving government officials a clear grounding in the financial system, regulatory architecture, international standards and the policy levers government holds.
programmes.intro: This training programme equips ministers, officials and public bodies with a clear understanding of how the financial system works, how it is regulated and the policy levers government holds over it.
programmes.track: G1. Financial Services Policy for Government

sections.Aim and Purpose:
To give officials in finance ministries, treasuries and other public bodies a practical, non-technical grounding in the financial system, the architecture of financial regulation and the respective roles of government and independent regulators. Participants leave able to frame financial services policy, ask the right questions of regulators and industry, and represent the national interest in international standard-setting and peer review.

**Coverage:** How the financial system works, the economic case for regulation, regulatory architecture and models, independence and accountability of regulators, international standards and peer reviews, banking, insurance, securities and payments, financial stability, financial crime, the policy levers available to government, and designing a national financial services policy.
sections.Intended Audience:
- Officials in finance ministries and treasuries responsible for financial services, banking and capital markets policy
- Senior officials and advisers to ministers who oversee or appoint financial regulators
- Staff of public agencies, cabinet offices and parliamentary committees who work on financial sector issues
sections.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the programme, participants will be able to:

- Explain how the financial system channels savings into investment and where it can fail
- Compare the main models of regulatory architecture and their strengths and weaknesses
- Distinguish the roles of government and independent regulators and design effective accountability
- Explain the international standards and peer review processes that apply to the national system
- Identify the policy levers available to government and the trade-offs between them
- Design the elements of a coherent national financial services policy
sections.Syllabus:
### Module 1: How the Financial System Works

The core functions of the financial system, the main institutions and markets that perform them, and how money, credit and risk flow through the economy.

**Objectives**

- Explain the economic functions of banks, insurers, markets and payment systems
- Describe how institutions and markets connect households, firms and government
- Identify the links between the financial sector, public finances and growth

**Syllabus**

- Intermediation, maturity transformation, risk transfer and payments
- Banks, insurers, pension schemes, funds and non-bank lenders
- Money, bond, equity and derivatives markets
- The financial sector's contribution to growth, tax and employment

### Module 2: Why Regulate: Market Failures and Policy Objectives

The economic case for financial regulation, the objectives regulators pursue, and the tensions between stability, consumer protection, market integrity, competition and growth.

**Objectives**

- Explain the market failures that justify financial regulation
- Distinguish prudential, conduct, market integrity and financial crime objectives
- Assess the trade-offs between regulatory objectives and economic growth

**Syllabus**

- Information asymmetry, externalities, moral hazard and contagion
- Statutory objectives and how they are framed in legislation
- Competition and growth objectives: benefits and risks
- Lessons from crises on the cost of regulatory failure

### Module 3: Regulatory Architecture: Models and Choices

How countries organise financial regulation, from sectoral and integrated regulators to twin peaks models, and the role of central banks, ministries and other public bodies.

**Objectives**

- Compare sectoral, integrated, twin peaks and hybrid models
- Explain the role of the central bank in prudential and macroprudential policy
- Evaluate coordination arrangements between authorities

**Syllabus**

- Sectoral, integrated and twin peaks models compared
- Central banks, financial stability committees and deposit insurers
- Memoranda of understanding and inter-agency coordination
- Case studies of architecture reform after a crisis

### Module 4: Independence and Accountability of Regulators

Why regulators are made operationally independent, the safeguards that protect independence, and how government and legislators hold regulators to account without undermining it.

**Objectives**

- Explain the rationale for operational independence and the risks of political interference
- Design governance, appointment, funding and legal protection arrangements
- Apply accountability tools such as reporting, performance review and parliamentary scrutiny

**Syllabus**

- Independence in international standards: what is expected
- Board composition, appointments, dismissal and funding models
- Annual reports, remit letters, performance frameworks and audit
- Questions government should ask its regulators

### Module 5: International Standards, Standard-Setters and Peer Reviews

The international bodies that set financial standards, how those standards bind or influence national policy, and how assessments and peer reviews judge a country's framework.

**Objectives**

- Describe the roles of the G20, FSB, BCBS, IOSCO, IAIS, CPMI and FATF
- Explain how standards are developed and how government can influence them
- Prepare for IMF and World Bank assessments, FSB peer reviews and FATF evaluations

**Syllabus**

- The international financial architecture and its standard-setters
- Core principles for banking, insurance, securities and market infrastructure
- Financial sector assessments, peer reviews and mutual evaluations
- Implementing recommendations and managing reputational consequences

### Module 6: Banking, Insurance and Prudential Regulation

How banks and insurers are regulated for safety and soundness, what capital and liquidity rules aim to achieve, and the policy choices government faces in implementing them.

**Objectives**

- Explain the purpose of capital, liquidity and solvency requirements
- Assess proportionality choices for smaller and domestic institutions
- Identify the fiscal and growth implications of prudential policy

**Syllabus**

- Capital, leverage and liquidity standards for banks
- Solvency and policyholder protection for insurers
- Proportionality, local adaptation and timing of implementation
- Credit supply, lending to the economy and the cost of prudential rules

### Module 7: Capital Markets, Conduct and Consumer Protection

How securities markets, investment services and retail financial products are regulated, and the policy choices in balancing investor protection, market access and innovation.

**Objectives**

- Explain the regulation of issuers, intermediaries, funds and trading venues
- Describe conduct and consumer protection frameworks and redress mechanisms
- Assess where conduct failures create political and fiscal pressure

**Syllabus**

- Securities regulation: disclosure, market abuse and intermediaries
- Retail investor protection, suitability and product governance
- Complaints, ombudsman schemes and compensation arrangements
- Case studies of mis-selling scandals and the policy response

### Module 8: Financial Stability, Crisis Management and Financial Crime

The macroprudential framework, how failing institutions are resolved, and the national arrangements for combating money laundering, terrorist financing and sanctions evasion.

**Objectives**

- Explain systemic risk and the macroprudential tools available to authorities
- Describe resolution regimes, deposit insurance and the role of the finance ministry in a crisis
- Identify government's responsibilities for AML/CFT and sanctions

**Syllabus**

- Systemic risk, macroprudential tools and financial stability committees
- Resolution, bail-in, deposit insurance and the limits of public support
- National AML/CFT strategy, FATF standards and the national FIU
- Financial sanctions: implementation and enforcement

### Module 9: Policy Levers and Policy Design

The instruments government holds over the financial sector, from legislation and regulatory remits to tax, public ownership and market development, and how to design and evaluate policy using them.

**Objectives**

- Identify the legislative, fiscal, institutional and convening levers available
- Apply cost-benefit analysis and consultation to financial services policy
- Evaluate industry proposals and lobbying with appropriate scepticism

**Syllabus**

- Legislation, secondary rules and remit letters
- Tax policy, public guarantees, state-owned institutions and development banks
- Impact assessment, consultation and post-implementation review
- Managing industry engagement and avoiding regulatory capture

### Module 10: Designing a National Financial Services Policy

Brings the programme together by examining how a national financial services strategy is developed, how emerging issues are anticipated and how policy is translated into action.

**Objectives**

- Assess the national financial sector's strengths, vulnerabilities and priorities
- Anticipate emerging issues including digital assets, AI, climate and cyber risk
- Produce a policy action plan with clear roles for government and regulators

**Syllabus**

- Diagnosing the financial sector: evidence, data and assessments
- Emerging issues: digital assets, AI, sustainable finance and operational resilience
- Sequencing reforms and building institutional capacity
- Workshop: a national financial services policy action plan
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as an intensive programme over three to four days or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a plain-language briefing with case studies and policy discussion, and modules can be selected or tailored to the ministry's priorities.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of public policy or economic affairs is helpful. No technical background in finance or regulation is required.
sections.Core Reading:
- BCBS (2024), Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision
- IOSCO (2017), Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation
- IAIS (2019), Insurance Core Principles and Common Framework for the Supervision of Internationally Active Insurance Groups
- IMF (2021), Financial Sector Assessment Program Review: Towards a More Stable and Sustainable Financial System

programmes.title: FinTech Business Models: Understanding and Supervising Innovation
programmes.summary: A ten-module programme equipping supervisors and firm compliance teams to understand how FinTech business models make money, grow and fail, and to assess their risks.
programmes.intro: This training programme equips supervisors, and the compliance teams of innovative firms, to understand how FinTech business models make money, grow and fail, and to assess their consumer, financial crime, resilience and viability risks.
programmes.track: X5. Data & Technology as Supervisory Infrastructure

sections.Aim and Purpose:
To give supervisors a practical understanding of the main FinTech business models, from digital lending and neobanks to trading apps, insurtech and crypto on-ramps, and of the unit economics and funding dynamics that drive their behaviour. Participants leave able to read a FinTech's model the way a supervisor does, identify red flags early, and apply proportionate licensing, innovation-facilitation and wind-down tools.

**Coverage:** The FinTech landscape and unit economics, digital lending and buy now, pay later, neobanks, wallets and payment apps, crowdfunding and peer-to-peer platforms, robo-advice and trading apps, insurtech, crypto on-ramps and regtech, growth, funding and partnership-chain risk, consumer outcomes, financial crime and operational resilience, licensing, sandboxes and innovation hubs, and failure and wind-down.
sections.Intended Audience:
- Supervisors, authorisation and innovation-hub staff dealing with FinTech applicants and fast-growing digital firms
- Policy, consumer protection and financial crime specialists assessing new business models
- Compliance, risk and legal teams in FinTech firms who want to see their firm the way a supervisor does
sections.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the programme, participants will be able to:

- Explain how the main FinTech business models generate revenue, acquire customers and scale
- Analyse unit economics, cash burn and funding dependency as early indicators of fragility
- Assess consumer outcomes, financial crime and operational resilience risks specific to each model
- Evaluate partnership chains and where regulatory accountability sits within them
- Compare licensing approaches, sandboxes and innovation hubs and their supervisory trade-offs
- Plan a proportionate supervisory response to a FinTech in difficulty, through to orderly wind-down
sections.Syllabus:
### Module 1: The FinTech Landscape and Unit Economics

How FinTech firms create value, the main business model archetypes, and the unit economics every supervisor should read before judging a firm's viability and incentives.

**Objectives**

- Map the main FinTech archetypes and their revenue sources
- Interpret customer acquisition cost, lifetime value, take rates and contribution margin
- Identify where revenue models create conduct and prudential incentives

**Syllabus**

- Archetypes: lenders, payment apps, platforms, advisers and infrastructure providers
- Revenue models: interchange, interest, float, subscriptions, fees and data
- Unit economics: acquisition cost, lifetime value, churn and contribution margin
- Reading a pitch deck and business plan as a supervisor

### Module 2: Digital Lending and Buy Now, Pay Later

How algorithmic lenders and BNPL providers originate, fund and collect credit, where affordability and credit risk are mispriced, and what supervisors test in their models and outcomes.

**Objectives**

- Explain the origination, funding and collections models of digital lenders
- Assess affordability testing, credit models and arrears management
- Identify red flags in BNPL growth, merchant incentives and repeat borrowing

**Syllabus**

- Alternative data, automated credit decisions and model drift
- Funding through warehouse lines, forward flow and securitisation
- BNPL economics: merchant fees, late fees and stacked borrowing
- Collections practices and vulnerable borrowers

### Module 3: Neobanks, Digital Wallets and Payment Apps

The economics of app-based banks, e-money wallets and payment apps, the customer funds and safeguarding risks they carry, and why rapid growth often outpaces controls.

**Objectives**

- Explain neobank and wallet revenue models and the path to profitability
- Assess safeguarding, reconciliation and the protection of customer funds
- Evaluate control maturity against customer growth and transaction volumes

**Syllabus**

- Deposit-taking neobanks versus e-money and payment licences
- Interchange dependency, float income and premium subscriptions
- Safeguarding, reconciliation and reliance on partner banks
- Red flags: onboarding surges, complaint spikes and account freezes

### Module 4: Crowdfunding and Peer-to-Peer Platforms

How lending and investment crowdfunding platforms match investors with borrowers and issuers, where conflicts and credit risk sit, and how supervisors test due diligence and client money arrangements.

**Objectives**

- Explain platform models for lending, equity and real estate crowdfunding
- Assess project due diligence, risk disclosure and investor protections
- Identify conflicts of interest and platform failure risks for investors

**Syllabus**

- Platform roles: introducer, servicer, guarantor or balance-sheet lender
- Credit assessment, provision funds and default reporting
- Investor categorisation, appropriateness and concentration limits
- Back-up servicing and continuity of loan books

### Module 5: Robo-Advice and Trading Apps

How automated advice and commission-free trading apps make money, how digital design shapes investor behaviour, and what supervisors examine in suitability, order handling and gamification.

**Objectives**

- Explain robo-advice and trading app revenue models, including payment for order flow
- Assess suitability algorithms, risk profiling and portfolio rebalancing
- Evaluate gamification, leverage and complex product access for retail investors

**Syllabus**

- Hybrid and fully automated advice models
- Commission-free trading, spreads, securities lending and order routing
- Gamification, push notifications and copy trading
- Supervisory testing of algorithms and customer journeys

### Module 6: Insurtech, Crypto On-Ramps and Regtech

Three fast-moving models: digital insurance distribution and pricing, fiat-to-crypto on-ramps embedded in consumer apps, and regtech providers that firms increasingly rely on for compliance.

**Objectives**

- Assess insurtech pricing, distribution and claims models for fair value
- Identify consumer and financial crime risks at crypto on-ramps
- Evaluate firms' reliance on regtech for onboarding, monitoring and reporting

**Syllabus**

- Usage-based and embedded insurance, data-driven pricing and claims automation
- On-ramp models: card and bank purchases of crypto inside consumer apps
- Regtech for identity, screening, monitoring and regulatory reporting
- Accountability when compliance is delivered by a technology vendor

### Module 7: Growth, Funding and Partnership-Chain Risk

How venture funding, cash burn and growth targets shape behaviour, and how chains of licensed providers, agents, programme managers and vendors blur accountability for customers and controls.

**Objectives**

- Analyse runway, cash burn and dependence on further funding rounds
- Map partnership chains and identify who holds the licence and the risk
- Recognise how growth pressure erodes controls and culture

**Syllabus**

- Funding stages, down rounds, valuation pressure and investor influence
- Runway, burn multiples and early warning indicators of distress
- Licence-holders, agents, distributors and outsourced compliance
- Founder-led governance and growth-at-all-costs culture

### Module 8: Consumer Outcomes, Financial Crime and Operational Resilience

The cross-cutting risks that recur across FinTech models: harm from digital journeys, exploitation by fraudsters and launderers, and fragile technology stacks built for speed rather than resilience.

**Objectives**

- Assess consumer outcomes, vulnerability and complaints across digital journeys
- Evaluate onboarding, fraud and transaction monitoring controls at scale
- Judge the resilience of technology stacks, cloud reliance and incident response

**Syllabus**

- Frictionless journeys, dark patterns and fair value
- Remote onboarding, synthetic identities, mule accounts and authorised push payment fraud
- Cloud dependency, change management and outage history
- Supervisory data and early warning indicators across the three risks

### Module 9: Licensing Approaches, Sandboxes and Innovation Hubs

How authorities licence FinTech activities, the design and limits of regulatory sandboxes and innovation hubs, and how to support innovation without lowering standards or creating moral hazard.

**Objectives**

- Compare full, restricted, phased and activity-based licensing approaches
- Evaluate the design, governance and outcomes of sandboxes and innovation hubs
- Identify the conflicts and moral hazard risks of innovation facilitation

**Syllabus**

- Perimeter questions and choosing the right licence
- Sandbox entry criteria, safeguards, testing parameters and exit
- Innovation hubs, cross-border testing networks and regtech challenges
- Avoiding implicit endorsement and regulatory capture

### Module 10: Failure, Wind-Down and Supervisory Workshop

How FinTechs fail, what an orderly wind-down requires for customers and their funds, and a workshop applying the programme to a fast-growing firm heading into difficulty.

**Objectives**

- Identify failure patterns in FinTech firms and their early signals
- Assess solvent wind-down plans and the protection of customer funds and data
- Apply the programme to a supervisory case involving a FinTech under stress

**Syllabus**

- Failure patterns: funding withdrawal, partner exit, fraud losses and control breakdown
- Wind-down planning, client money return and continuity of critical services
- Supervisory intervention, communication and coordination with other authorities
- Workshop: a fast-growing FinTech loses its funding and partner bank
sections.Structure and Format: Ten modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a multi-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a briefing with case studies, business model analysis exercises and supervisory question sets, closing with a FinTech failure workshop, and modules can be selected or tailored to the client's needs.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of supervision, authorisation or compliance in financial services is helpful. No technical or financial modelling background is required.
sections.Core Reading:
- FATF, Opportunities and Challenges of New Technologies for AML/CFT (2021)
- G20/OECD High-Level Principles on Financial Consumer Protection (2022)
- FSB, The Use of Supervisory and Regulatory Technology by Authorities and Regulated Institutions (2020)
- FATF, Guidance on Digital Identity (2020)

programmes.title: Fit and Proper Assessments: Approving Owners, Directors and Key Function Holders
programmes.summary: An eight-module practitioner programme on assessing owners, controllers, directors and key function holders, from evidence gathering and interviews to defensible decisions.
programmes.intro: This training programme equips authorisation and supervisory staff to assess the fitness and propriety of owners, controllers, directors and key function holders with rigour, consistency and well-evidenced decisions.

sections.Aim and Purpose:
To give authorisation and supervisory staff a practical, end-to-end method for fit and proper assessments, from controllers and qualifying holdings through source of wealth to competence, capacity and approval interviews. Participants leave able to gather and test evidence, reach defensible decisions, impose conditions or refuse where necessary, and monitor fitness on an ongoing basis.

**Coverage:** The fit and proper test and its components, controllers and qualifying holdings, source of wealth and source of funds, honesty and integrity, competence and capacity, approval interviews, conditions, refusals and procedural fairness, ongoing fitness and reassessment, and a case workshop.
sections.Intended Audience:
- Authorisation and licensing staff responsible for approving owners, directors and key function holders
- Supervisors and inspectors who assess changes in control or monitor ongoing fitness
- Enforcement and legal staff involved in fitness-related decisions and challenges
sections.Learning Objectives:
By the end of the programme, participants will be able to:

- Explain the purpose and components of the fit and proper test and the standards behind it
- Assess controllers, qualifying holdings and ownership chains, including beneficial ownership
- Evaluate source of wealth and source of funds evidence critically
- Assess the competence, capacity, honesty and integrity of directors and key function holders
- Plan and conduct effective approval interviews
- Reach, record and communicate defensible decisions, including conditions and refusals
sections.Syllabus:
### Module 1: The Fit and Proper Test: Purpose and Standards

Why the authority assesses the fitness and propriety of owners and individuals, the components of the test and the international standards that underpin it.

**Objectives**

- Explain the purpose of fit and proper assessments in protecting firms and markets
- Describe the components of the test: integrity, competence, capacity and financial soundness
- Apply the burden and standard of proof to fitness decisions

**Syllabus**

- The gateway's role in preventing harm before it occurs
- Honesty, integrity, reputation, competence, capability and financial soundness
- International standards from the Basel Committee, IOSCO, IAIS and FATF
- Burden of proof, proportionality and consistency of decisions

### Module 2: Controllers, Qualifying Holdings and Ownership Chains

How to identify who owns and controls an applicant firm, assess proposed acquirers and see through complex or opaque ownership structures.

**Objectives**

- Identify controllers, qualifying holdings and ultimate beneficial owners
- Assess proposed acquirers and changes in control
- Recognise structures designed to obscure ownership or influence

**Syllabus**

- Control thresholds, acting in concert and indirect holdings
- Mapping ownership chains and identifying beneficial owners
- Assessing acquirers: reputation, financial soundness and strategy
- Red flags: nominees, trusts, layered structures and secrecy jurisdictions

### Module 3: Source of Wealth and Source of Funds

How to test where an owner's wealth and the funds for an acquisition or capital injection come from, and when the evidence is not good enough.

**Objectives**

- Distinguish source of wealth from source of funds
- Evaluate the credibility and sufficiency of supporting evidence
- Identify financial crime risks in funding arrangements

**Syllabus**

- Building a wealth narrative and testing its plausibility
- Documentary evidence: what to request and how to verify it
- Borrowed funds, complex financing and politically exposed persons
- Red flags and when to refer concerns to financial crime specialists

### Module 4: Honesty, Integrity and Reputation

How to assess the integrity of individuals and owners, the checks the authority should carry out and how to weigh past conduct and disclosures.

**Objectives**

- Design proportionate background and due diligence checks
- Assess the relevance and seriousness of past conduct
- Respond to non-disclosure, misleading information and adverse findings

**Syllabus**

- Criminal, regulatory, civil and insolvency checks
- Open-source research and information from other authorities
- Weighing seriousness, recency, pattern and rehabilitation
- Non-disclosure as a fitness issue in its own right

### Module 5: Competence, Capability and Capacity

How to assess whether directors and key function holders have the knowledge, experience and time to perform their roles, individually and as a board.

**Objectives**

- Assess competence against the specific role and the firm's risk profile
- Evaluate time commitment, multiple directorships and conflicts of interest
- Consider the collective suitability of the board and senior team

**Syllabus**

- Role profiles, experience and qualifications
- Capacity, other commitments and conflicts of interest
- Collective suitability, board composition and independence
- Key function holders: risk, compliance, MLRO and finance

### Module 6: Conducting Approval Interviews

How to plan and conduct interviews with proposed directors and key function holders that test competence and understanding rather than recitation.

**Objectives**

- Plan an approval interview with clear objectives and lines of questioning
- Use open and probing questions to test knowledge and judgement
- Record the interview and its conclusions as evidence

**Syllabus**

- Preparing the interview plan from the application file
- Scenario-based and probing questions for different roles
- Assessing answers: depth, ownership and red flags
- Role-play: interviewing a proposed chief executive and compliance officer

### Module 7: Decisions: Approvals, Conditions and Refusals

How to reach, document and communicate fit and proper decisions, including conditional approvals, withdrawals and refusals, with procedural fairness.

**Objectives**

- Weigh evidence to reach a reasoned and defensible decision
- Design conditions and undertakings that are clear and enforceable
- Apply procedural fairness when minded to refuse

**Syllabus**

- Structuring the decision paper and recommendation
- Conditional approvals, undertakings and restrictions
- Minded-to-refuse processes, representations and appeals
- Encouraging withdrawal and recording the rationale

### Module 8: Ongoing Fitness and Case Workshop

How fitness is monitored after approval and when reassessment is required, followed by a workshop in which participants work a complete case to a decision.

**Objectives**

- Identify triggers for reassessing fitness during supervision
- Coordinate with supervision and enforcement on fitness concerns
- Apply the full assessment method to a realistic case

**Syllabus**

- Ongoing obligations, notifications and annual certifications
- Triggers for reassessment and removal of approval
- Linking gateway findings to supervisory priorities
- Workshop: assessing a change in control and a director application to decision
sections.Structure and Format: Eight modules of about three hours each, delivered in person, virtually or in a hybrid format, either as a four-day programme or as a series of half-day sessions. Each module combines a short briefing with realistic application files, interview role-play and decision exercises, and modules can be selected or tailored to the authority's processes.
sections.Useful Prior Knowledge and Experience: Some experience of authorisation, licensing or supervisory work is helpful. Participants new to the gateway may benefit from attending a foundation programme first.
sections.Core Reading:
- Basel Committee on Banking Supervision (2024), Core Principles for Effective Banking Supervision
- IAIS (2019, as updated), Insurance Core Principles and Common Framework for the Supervision of Internationally Active Insurance Groups
- IOSCO (2017), Objectives and Principles of Securities Regulation
- FATF (2023), Guidance on Beneficial Ownership of Legal Persons
